---
title: "Time trends and percentage change"
subtitle: "Reading changes in levels, growth rates, and composition without confusing stocks with flows"
---

::: {.callout-note title="Learning goals"}
Build a destination–year dataset; read and construct line charts; compare **levels**, **absolute changes**, **percentage changes**, and **indexed series**; use facets and bar charts to tell different parts of a time-series story; calculate year-on-year changes with `lag()`; recognize missing years and changing data coverage; distinguish what a trend shows from what could have caused it.
:::

## Why study change over time?

In previous chapters, we described differences **between places in a particular year**. We now add a second dimension: **time**. Instead of asking only how many refugees were recorded in Germany in 2022, we can ask how the reported stock changed between 2015 and 2022, whether changes were gradual or abrupt, and whether the trajectories differed from those of France and Spain.

A **cross-section** compares units at one point in time. A **time series** follows a variable for the same unit over time. When we follow *several* destinations across *several* years, we have a simple **panel dataset**: each observation represents a *destination–year*.

| Question | What we need | Useful display |
|---|---|---|
| How many refugees were reported in each destination in each year? | **Levels** | Line chart |
| Which country experienced the largest numerical increase? | **Absolute changes** | Change table or bars |
| Which country grew most relative to its starting level? | **Percentage changes** | Indexed line chart |
| Did a particular year bring an unusually large change? | **Year-on-year changes** | Annual-change bars |
| Were trajectories similar, or did they differ in timing? | **Within-country patterns** | Small-multiple line charts |
| Which origin groups account for recorded stocks in one destination? | **Composition** | Stacked area chart |

::: {.callout-important title="The interpretation comes before the graph"}
We will use the `refugees` package's **end-of-year `refugees` population stock**, not annual arrivals, applications lodged, or asylum decisions. The tables are compiled from statistical reporting systems that may evolve. This chapter is an exercise in descriptive analysis, not evidence that one country's policies *caused* its trajectory.
:::

## Begin with two different meanings of 'change'

Consider two **fictional** destinations:

| Destination | 2015 stock | 2022 stock | Increase in persons | Percentage increase |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 100,000 | 200,000 | 100,000 | 100% |
| B | 1,000,000 | 1,300,000 | 300,000 | 30% |

Destination B gained more people in **absolute** terms, but destination A had the larger **relative** increase. Neither description is wrong; they answer different questions.

For a variable with values $x_{t-1}$ and $x_t$:

$$\text{Absolute change}_t = x_t-x_{t-1}$$

$$\text{Percentage change}_t = 100\left(\frac{x_t}{x_{t-1}}-1\right).$$

The first is measured in **persons**; the second is measured in **percent**. These are not interchangeable. A percentage change is undefined if the initial value is zero.

```{r}
# Fictional values to practise the formulas
old_stock <- 100000
new_stock <- 200000

new_stock - old_stock
100 * (new_stock / old_stock - 1)
```

**Predict, then run:** If an observed stock falls from 200,000 to 160,000, what is the absolute change? What is the percentage change? Why is the percentage negative?

## Prepare the UNHCR data: from origin–destination–year to destination–year

We'll use the same three destinations throughout: **Germany, France, and Spain**, from **2015 to 2022**. A fixed time window helps us compare like with like, although some historical comparability issues remain.

```{r}
library(refugees)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

pop <- refugees::population

series <- pop |>
  filter(
    year >= 2015,
    year <= 2022,
    coa_iso %in% c("DEU", "FRA", "ESP")
  ) |>
  group_by(coa_iso, coa_name, year) |>
  summarise(
    # Avoid interpreting an entirely missing group as zero.
    stock = if (all(is.na(refugees))) {
      NA_real_
    } else {
      sum(refugees, na.rm = TRUE)
    },
    origin_rows = n(),
    missing_cells = sum(is.na(refugees)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(coa_iso, year)

head(series, 10)
```

**Read the pipeline in words:** keep three destinations and eight years; group records by *destination and year*; add the origin-specific stocks within each group; record some information about data coverage; sort by destination and date.

The new table contains one row for each recorded **destination–year**. In contrast, the original `population` table usually has multiple origins within a given destination–year. If we failed to aggregate across origins, a line chart could display many observations for a single destination and year.

::: {.callout-tip title="Why keep `origin_rows` and `missing_cells`?"}
They help us check the data. The number of origin records may change over time, and a sum with some missing entries may be incomplete. Also, `sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)` returns zero if *all* the values in `x` are missing; our additional `if` statement preserves that distinction. These checks do **not** by themselves establish that every year's coverage is comparable.
:::

### Check the time series before plotting

```{r}
series |>
  group_by(coa_name) |>
  summarise(
    first_year = min(year),
    last_year = max(year),
    years_observed = n_distinct(year),
    missing_stock_years = sum(is.na(stock)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# There should be at most one row per destination and year.
series |>
  count(coa_iso, year) |>
  filter(n > 1)
```

The second command should return an **empty table**: after aggregation we expect only one row per destination–year. The first command checks the number of years and whether any resulting stock is missing. A complete 2015–2022 annual series has eight years. We should not assume completeness without checking it.

## Graph 1: compare the levels with a line chart

A line chart is often the first useful graph for a time series. Time runs from left to right; the height of the line shows the observed quantity. We connect observations to make changes easier to see.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stock-levels
#| fig-cap: "Reported end-of-year refugee stocks for Germany, France, and Spain, 2015–2022. Source: UNHCR data distributed through the refugees R package; destination–year totals sum recorded origin rows."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(series, aes(x = year, y = stock / 1e6, color = coa_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2022) +
  labs(
    title = "Refugee stocks in three destinations",
    subtitle = "End-of-year counts, expressed in millions",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Refugees (millions)",
    color = "Destination"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

**How to read @fig-stock-levels:**

1. Identify the **unit** on the vertical axis: millions of people, not percentages.
2. Compare the heights of the lines in a given year (**between-country levels**).
3. Follow one line from left to right (**within-country change**).
4. Note changes in slope or apparent breaks, without immediately assigning them a cause.

A line segment connects two annual observations; we have not observed every day between them. Annual figures do not reveal *when within the year* the changes occurred.

::: {.callout-warning title="Do not read a mechanism into a trend"}
An upward-sloping line does not demonstrate an increase in asylum applications, recognition rates, or arrivals. It shows only an increase in the **reported end-of-year stock** for the selected category. Investigating causes would require additional data, definitions, and a research design.
:::

## Graph 2: small multiples reveal the shape of each trajectory

When one country has a much larger stock than another, the smaller line may appear almost flat on a shared axis. A **facet** gives each destination its own panel.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stock-facets
#| fig-cap: "The same destination–year stock data in separate panels. The vertical scales differ, so compare the pattern within each panel rather than line heights across panels."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

ggplot(series, aes(x = year, y = stock / 1e6)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2475a6", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#2475a6", size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ coa_name, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2015, 2017, 2019, 2021, 2022)) +
  labs(
    title = "Reading each country's trajectory separately",
    subtitle = "Notice that every panel has its own vertical scale",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Refugees (millions)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

`facet_wrap(~ coa_name)` creates one panel per destination, and `scales = "free_y"` allows each panel to use a different vertical scale. This is useful for seeing **within-country variation**, but it makes direct comparison of the *size* of changes less intuitive. Compare @fig-stock-facets with @fig-stock-levels: the same data can emphasize different features depending on the graphical choices.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try the alternative"}
Change `scales = "free_y"` to `scales = "fixed"`, or remove that argument. Which version makes it easier to compare **levels across countries**? Which makes it easier to see **changes within countries**? Neither version is universally better.
:::

## Graph 3: compare the beginning and the end of the period

Another way to summarize a trajectory is to focus on two selected years. This loses information about what happened in between, but makes the comparison of levels clear.

```{r}
endpoints <- series |>
  filter(year %in% c(2015, 2022)) |>
  mutate(year_label = factor(year))

endpoints |>
  select(coa_name, year, stock)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-endpoint-bars
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of reported stock levels in 2015 and 2022; intermediate-year changes are not shown."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(
  endpoints,
  aes(x = coa_name, y = stock / 1e6, fill = year_label)
) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "How different were the beginning and end?",
    x = "Destination",
    y = "Refugees (millions)",
    fill = "Year"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

`geom_col()` uses the stock values already calculated. `position = "dodge"` places the two years side by side rather than stacking them. Notice what this graph **cannot** show: a country might have risen and then fallen between the endpoints.

## Graph 4: indexed series put different starting levels on a comparable scale

The level chart answers **how many?** But when starting values differ greatly, we may instead ask **how much did each series change relative to where it began?**

An **index with 2015 = 100** solves that graphical problem:

$$I_t = 100\times\frac{\text{Stock}_t}{\text{Stock}_{2015}}.$$

An index value of 100 means the same level as in 2015; 120 means **20% above the 2015 level**; 80 means **20% below the 2015 level**. The index is **not** a percentage share of the world's refugees.

```{r}
indexed <- series |>
  group_by(coa_iso, coa_name) |>
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    base_2015 = stock[year == 2015][1],
    index_2015 = if_else(
      !is.na(base_2015) & base_2015 > 0,
      100 * stock / base_2015,
      NA_real_
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

indexed |>
  filter(year %in% c(2015, 2022)) |>
  select(coa_name, year, stock, index_2015)
```

This example assumes that every destination has a 2015 observation. We checked the time coverage earlier; if 2015 were missing, we would need to choose a different common baseline or leave the index undefined.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stock-index
#| fig-cap: "Indexed reported refugee stocks (2015 = 100). Each line is scaled relative to that destination's own 2015 stock, so relative movements—not absolute stock levels—are comparable."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(indexed, aes(year, index_2015, color = coa_name)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2022) +
  labs(
    title = "How did stocks change relative to 2015?",
    subtitle = "Each destination starts at an index value of 100",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Index (2015 = 100)",
    color = "Destination"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

Compare @fig-stock-index with @fig-stock-levels. A destination can have the **highest index growth** and still have the **smallest number of refugees**. The indexed figure changes the measurement scale; it does not change the underlying data.

::: {.callout-note title="An index is not a growth rate"}
If a destination's index is 150 in 2022, its 2022 stock is **50% higher than its 2015 stock**. It does **not** mean the stock increased by 50% *in 2022*, or by 50% *every year*. We must specify the baseline year.
:::

## Calculate year-on-year changes with `lag()`

To measure change **between consecutive years**, we need the previous observation for the *same destination*. We use `group_by()` to make that comparison within countries, `arrange()` to put years in chronological order, and `lag()` to retrieve the previous value.

```{r}
series_changes <- series |>
  group_by(coa_iso, coa_name) |>
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    previous_year = lag(year),
    previous_stock = lag(stock),
    absolute_change = if_else(
      year - previous_year == 1,
      stock - previous_stock,
      NA_real_
    ),
    percent_change = if_else(
      year - previous_year == 1 & previous_stock > 0,
      100 * (stock / previous_stock - 1),
      NA_real_
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

series_changes |>
  filter(coa_iso == "ESP") |>
  select(year, stock, previous_stock, absolute_change, percent_change)
```

The first year is missing a prior observation within the chosen window, so its annual changes are `NA`. We also check that `year - previous_year == 1`: otherwise, `lag()` might compare **2018 with 2016** and mistakenly label that a one-year change. Percentage change is additionally undefined for a starting value of zero.

`NA_real_` creates a missing value of numeric type. This helps `if_else()` construct a consistently numeric column. A missing rate is not necessarily a zero rate.

## Graph 5: annual absolute changes show when reported stocks rose or fell

A plot of **levels** can disguise important changes in slope. We can instead graph the *difference between years* as a sequence of bars, including negative bars for decreases.

```{r}
#| label: fig-annual-differences
#| fig-cap: "Year-on-year changes in recorded refugee stocks, in millions of people. These are differences between two end-of-year stocks, not counts of arrivals."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

ggplot(
  series_changes |> filter(!is.na(absolute_change)),
  aes(x = factor(year), y = absolute_change / 1e6)
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
  geom_col(fill = "#2475a6", width = 0.75) +
  facet_wrap(~ coa_name, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "In which years were changes largest?",
    subtitle = "Positive and negative differences in reported end-of-year stocks",
    x = "Year (compared with previous year)",
    y = "Change in stock (millions)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

In @fig-annual-differences, the zero line matters. Bars above zero indicate a larger reported stock than one year earlier; bars below zero indicate a smaller one. An unusually tall bar is a **descriptive finding** worth investigating, not proof of a particular event or policy mechanism.

## Graph 6: annual percentage changes tell a different story

The percentage change uses the previous year's stock as the **denominator**. This makes the rate more comparable across places of different sizes, but can give very large values when the denominator is small.

```{r}
#| label: fig-annual-growth
#| fig-cap: "Year-on-year percentage changes in recorded refugee stocks. Percentages refer to each destination's stock in the preceding year."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

ggplot(
  series_changes |> filter(!is.na(percent_change)),
  aes(x = factor(year), y = percent_change)
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
  geom_col(fill = "#bf642b", width = 0.75) +
  facet_wrap(~ coa_name, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Percentage changes depend on the previous year's stock",
    x = "Year (compared with previous year)",
    y = "Annual percentage change (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

Compare @fig-annual-growth with @fig-annual-differences. A year with the biggest **absolute change** does not necessarily have the biggest **percentage change**. In addition, `scales = "free_y"` changes the vertical scale across panels, so equal-looking bar heights need not represent equal percentages.

::: {.callout-warning title="Three different percentages"}
Keep these distinct:

- **Growth rate:** from 100,000 to 120,000 is an increase of **20%**.
- **Percentage-point difference:** from a 30% recognition rate to a 40% recognition rate is an increase of **10 percentage points**.
- **Percentage share:** 120,000 out of 600,000 is a **20% share** of the specified total.

All use the symbol `%`, but their numerators, denominators, and interpretations differ.
:::

## One compact table: compare overall changes from 2015 to 2022

A final table makes it easy to answer which destination had the largest numerical change and which had the largest change relative to its starting value.

```{r}
period_summary <- series |>
  group_by(coa_iso, coa_name) |>
  summarise(
    stock_2015 = stock[year == 2015][1],
    stock_2022 = stock[year == 2022][1],
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    change_persons = stock_2022 - stock_2015,
    change_percent = if_else(
      !is.na(stock_2015) & stock_2015 > 0,
      100 * (stock_2022 / stock_2015 - 1),
      NA_real_
    )
  )

period_summary |>
  select(coa_name, stock_2015, stock_2022,
         change_persons, change_percent) |>
  arrange(desc(change_persons))
```

Why calculate changes from the endpoints rather than add up annual growth rates? **Percentage growth rates generally cannot be added across years.** Absolute yearly differences *can* be added to recover the endpoint difference if the sequence is complete and consistent: intermediate increases and decreases cancel out.

### A simple check with fictional numbers

Suppose the stock rises from 100 to 120, then from 120 to 132. The two annual increases are 20% and 10%, but the total increase is **32%**, not 30%:

```{r}
(120 / 100 - 1) * 100
(132 / 120 - 1) * 100
(132 / 100 - 1) * 100
```

The changes **compound** because the second percentage uses a new denominator. We will return to related issues when we study statistical modeling and the interpretation of coefficients.

## Graph 7: examine the changing composition of one destination's stock

A total can change for different reasons. Even when the overall stock rises, the relative importance of **recorded origin categories** may shift. One way to examine this is with a **stacked area chart**.

Here we look at Germany and identify the **four largest recorded origin codes in 2022**. We group all other recorded origins together so the chart remains readable.

```{r}
germany_origins <- pop |>
  filter(
    coa_iso == "DEU",
    year >= 2015,
    year <= 2022
  ) |>
  group_by(year, coo_iso, coo_name) |>
  summarise(
    stock = sum(refugees, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

largest_2022 <- germany_origins |>
  filter(year == 2022) |>
  slice_max(order_by = stock, n = 4, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  pull(coo_iso)

germany_composition <- germany_origins |>
  mutate(
    origin_group = if_else(
      coo_iso %in% largest_2022,
      coo_name,
      "Other recorded origins"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(year, origin_group) |>
  summarise(stock = sum(stock, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

germany_composition |>
  filter(year == 2022) |>
  arrange(desc(stock))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-germany-composition
#| fig-cap: "Composition of Germany's recorded end-of-year refugee stock by four origin codes selected using the 2022 ranking and a residual category. Categories selected by 2022 size do not necessarily dominate earlier years."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5

ggplot(
  germany_composition,
  aes(x = year, y = stock / 1e6, fill = origin_group)
) +
  geom_area(position = "stack", alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2022) +
  labs(
    title = "How did the recorded origin composition change?",
    subtitle = "Germany: four leading origin codes in 2022 versus all other origins",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Recorded refugee stock (millions)",
    fill = "Origin group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

A stacked area chart answers a different question from the line chart. It shows which groups contribute to the **total observed stock** at each point in time. A wider band means a larger recorded stock in that group. It does **not** show the number of arrivals from that origin in that year. Group definitions, unknown origins, or reporting changes can complicate the interpretation.

::: {.callout-tip title="How is this connected to the previous chapters?"}
We first **filter** for Germany, then **group and summarize** by origin and year, **select** the largest origin categories in 2022, **mutate** a simpler classification, and finally display the result with `ggplot2`. The same core functions now help answer a richer research question.
:::

## What these figures can—and cannot—tell us

| Observation in a graph | Supported descriptive statement | Interpretation that needs more evidence |
|---|---|---|
| A line rises | The reported end-of-year stock increased | More people arrived through a specific route |
| A bar is negative | The next end-of-year stock is smaller | A policy caused departures or returns |
| An index rises rapidly | The stock grew rapidly relative to its baseline | This country offered more effective protection |
| One origin band expands | A larger stock is reported in that origin category | The same number of new people arrived that year |
| A large change appears in 2022 | A change in reported levels is visible | One particular international event explains all of it |

Several mechanisms can affect a population stock: new arrivals, departures, returns, births, deaths, recognition or classification changes, registration practices, and statistical revisions. **The difference between two stocks is not a direct measure of any one of these components.**

For source definitions, consult the [`refugees` package documentation](https://populationstatistics.github.io/refugees/reference/population.html) and the [UNHCR Refugee Data Finder](https://www.unhcr.org/refugee-statistics/).

## A checklist for responsible time-series analysis

Before interpreting or presenting a time-series chart, ask:

1. **Unit:** What does one row represent—an origin–destination–year, a destination–year, or something else?
2. **Category:** Are we consistently following `refugees`, `asylum_seekers`, or another population group?
3. **Time:** Are all points measured at the end of the year, or are we mixing stocks and annual flows?
4. **Coverage:** Are there missing years or origin cells? Did definitions or recording practices change?
5. **Denominator:** Are we plotting numbers, percentage changes, a share, or an index? What is the baseline?
6. **Graph:** Does the chosen axis and scale permit the comparison we claim?
7. **Interpretation:** Which findings are descriptive, and which explanations are only hypotheses?

## Exercises: predict, compute, visualize, explain

### A. Understand the numbers

1. A hypothetical stock rises from 80,000 to 100,000. Calculate the **absolute change** and **percentage change** by hand, then verify with R.
2. Calculate the 2015 and 2022 stocks for each of the three destinations in `period_summary`. Which destination has the largest **absolute** increase? Which has the largest **relative** increase? Are they the same?
3. Suppose an index is 185 in 2022, with 2015 = 100. Write one accurate sentence about its interpretation. What can you *not* conclude?
4. Explain why two successive annual growth rates of +20% and +10% do not equal a total increase of +30%.

### B. Explore the figures

5. Reproduce @fig-stock-levels using only **Germany and Spain**. Which statement becomes easier to see?
6. Change the period from **2015–2022** to **2018–2022** by modifying the original filter. How might selecting a different start year change the story? Remember that an index needs an explicitly selected baseline.
7. Compare @fig-stock-levels and @fig-stock-index. Explain what each displays in one sentence.
8. Reproduce @fig-stock-facets with `scales = "fixed"`. Which scale choice is more appropriate when your question concerns **between-country levels**?
9. In @fig-annual-differences and @fig-annual-growth, identify a year when **absolute and percentage change** give different impressions. Describe the denominator responsible for the difference.
10. Modify the composition chart to select the **three** largest origin codes in Germany in 2022. What changes in the chart, and what remains the same?

### C. Check and improve the code

11. Inspect `series_changes` and explain why the first year's `absolute_change` is missing. What would go wrong if we sorted years in the wrong order before using `lag()`?
12. Imagine that a destination has observations in **2018 and 2020 but none in 2019**. Why is it misleading to call `stock - lag(stock)` an annual change without checking the year gap?
13. Create a chart comparing the **end-of-year asylum-seeker stock** for the same three destinations, using `asylum_seekers` from the `population` table. Explain why these are still not annual applications.
14. Write an accurate caption for a chart of year-on-year changes. Include the **measure**, **unit**, **time period**, **geography**, and **source**.

### D. Research interpretation

15. Write a short paragraph that separates: **(a)** what a time-series graph shows; **(b)** a hypothesis about why it changed; and **(c)** the additional evidence needed to investigate the hypothesis. Avoid claiming that stocks equal arrivals or decisions.

::: {.callout-tip title="Take-home check"}
You understand this chapter when you can explain why two countries can have different rankings in **levels**, **absolute changes**, and **percentage changes**, produce at least two graphs of the same time series, and describe what each graph can and cannot establish.
:::
